title: Introduction to LLMs
subtitle: What large language models are and what they can do
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Developers hear about GPT, Claude, and Gemini constantly but don't know what they actually are under the hood — leading to misuse, unrealistic expectations, and poor integration decisions.
whyItExists.solution: Understanding LLMs as next-token predictors trained on massive text datasets reframes every capability and limitation in a logical, predictable way.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Before integrating any LLM API — this mental model governs every decision from prompt design to cost estimation.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: If you need deterministic, explainable logic (e.g. tax calculation), LLMs are the wrong tool — use rule engines or classical code.

explainModes.beginner: Imagine a super-smart autocomplete. You type a question, and it predicts the most useful next word, then the word after that, thousands of times — until a full answer appears. It learned this by reading most of the internet.
explainModes.simple: An LLM is a neural network trained on billions of text documents. It learns statistical patterns so well that it can generate coherent, useful text on almost any topic.
explainModes.standard: LLMs are transformer-based neural networks trained with self-supervised learning to predict the next token in a sequence. The training objective is deceptively simple but produces rich internal representations of knowledge.
explainModes.technical: Autoregressive decoder-only transformers (GPT architecture) learn a probability distribution P(token_n | token_1 ... token_{n-1}). After pretraining, RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) aligns the model to be helpful and safe.
explainModes.deepDive: The training process involves two phases: pretraining (predict next token on web-scale data) and alignment (SFT + RLHF or DPO). The resulting model has dense weight matrices that encode world knowledge as continuous geometry in high-dimensional space — meaning concepts with similar meaning are geometrically close.

content.text: What is a Large Language Model?

A Large Language Model (LLM) is a neural network trained on vast text corpora to predict the next token. Through this training they develop impressive language and reasoning abilities. Modern LLMs like claude-opus-4-5, GPT-4o, and Gemini 1.5 Pro can write code, answer questions, summarise documents, translate languages, and reason through complex problems.

content.definition: The basic unit an LLM processes. A token is roughly 4 characters or 0.75 words in English. 'ChatGPT is great!' is about 6 tokens. Code tends to use more tokens per character than prose.
The maximum number of tokens an LLM can process at once — including both the input (prompt + history) and output. Claude 3.5 Sonnet has a 200K token context window (~150,000 words).

content.text: How LLMs Work — the Core Loop

items: You send a text prompt (tokenised to integers)
The model runs the tokens through transformer layers (attention + feed-forward)
It outputs a probability distribution over its full vocabulary
The highest-probability token is selected (or sampled with temperature)
That token is appended to the context and the loop repeats until the response is complete

content.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY env var

message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Explain what an LLM is in one paragraph."}
    ]
)

print(message.content[0].text)
print(f"Tokens used — in: {message.usage.input_tokens}, out: {message.usage.output_tokens}")

a.name: Claude (Anthropic)
a.description: Constitutional AI, long context (200K), very strong at coding and analysis
a.useWhen: Long-document analysis, complex reasoning, enterprise safety requirements

b.name: GPT-4o (OpenAI)
b.description: Multi-modal (vision + audio), massive ecosystem, fine-tuning available
b.useWhen: Vision tasks, fine-tuning workflows, existing OpenAI-based infrastructure

content.text: LLMs are probabilistic. The same prompt can produce different outputs. Set temperature=0 for deterministic, reproducible results (best for extraction/classification). Use higher temperatures (0.7–1.0) for creative tasks.
LLMs can hallucinate — confidently state false information. Always validate LLM outputs that will be shown to users or used in automated pipelines, especially for facts, numbers, and citations.

content.code:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# Deterministic: use temperature=0 for classification/extraction
result = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-5-5",
    max_tokens=10,
    temperature=0,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Classify: 'I love this product!' -> POSITIVE or NEGATIVE?"}]
)
print(result.content[0].text)  # Always: POSITIVE

# Creative: use higher temperature
story = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-5-5",
    max_tokens=200,
    temperature=0.9,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write the first line of a sci-fi story."}]
)
print(story.content[0].text)  # Different every time

content.text: API pricing is per token. claude-haiku-5-5 costs ~$0.25/1M input tokens. claude-opus-4-5 costs ~$15/1M. For prototyping, always use Haiku or Sonnet to control costs.

questions.question: What is a token in the context of LLMs?
options: A security credential for API authentication
The basic unit of text processing — roughly 4 characters or 0.75 words
A type of neural network weight
questions.explanation: Tokens are the sub-word units LLMs process. English averages about 0.75 words per token. API pricing is charged per token.

questions.question: What does setting temperature=0 do to an LLM?
options: Makes the model pick the highest-probability token every time (deterministic)
Makes the model refuse to answer
questions.explanation: Temperature=0 selects the most probable token at each step, making output reproducible. Use it for classification, extraction, and any task needing consistent answers.

questions.question: Why do LLMs hallucinate?
options: They have bugs in the code
They generate plausible-sounding text based on patterns, not factual lookup
They run out of memory mid-response
questions.explanation: LLMs generate text token-by-token based on learned patterns. They don't have a fact-checker — they produce what is statistically likely, which can be wrong.

faq.a: No intrinsic memory. You must include prior turns in the context window (messages array) to give the model conversation history.

faq.q: What is the difference between a base model and a chat model?
faq.a: A base model only does next-token prediction. A chat model has been fine-tuned with RLHF to follow instructions and be helpful. All commercially available models (Claude, GPT-4) are chat models.

faq.q: Which model should I start with?
faq.a: Start with claude-haiku-5-5 or gpt-4o-mini for cost-effective prototyping. Move to Sonnet or GPT-4o when you need higher quality. Use Opus/GPT-4 only when other models fall short.
